reason: E1 supports the need for surface modification and the suitability of laser cladding, but the specific claims about Ti(C,N) reinforcement achieving a twofold hardness increase and 50% wear reduction, as well as high-temperature performance, are not directly supported by the cited evidence. E3 only generally mentions hard particles in Ni-based alloys, and E2 highlights limitations of ceramic additions without confirming the proposed benefits.
premises: Titanium alloys have low hardness and poor wear resistance, motivating surface modification.
Laser cladding can produce metallurgically bonded composite coatings with hard ceramic phases.
In situ formed Ti(C,N) phases can double hardness and reduce wear by 50% in nickel-based coatings.
Optimized laser parameters can control residual stresses to prevent cracking.
The coating remains effective up to ~600°C in corrosive, high-wear environments.
